transcript:
```markdown
[doctor] Hi Ms. Gomez, how are you feeling today? What brings you in?

[patient] Hi doctor, I’ve been feeling really tired lately. I’m also going to the bathroom a lot and I'm always thirsty.

[doctor] Hmm, I see. How long have you been experiencing these symptoms?

[patient] It’s been about three weeks now, and it seems to be getting worse.

[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Can you describe how these symptoms are affecting your day-to-day life?

[patient] Well, I’m having a hard time concentrating at work because I’m so tired. It’s really frustrating.

[doctor] I understand. Have you noticed any weight loss or other changes?

[patient] No, I haven’t lost any weight. Just feeling really tired and thirsty all the time.

[doctor] Okay, and how would you rate the severity of your symptoms on a scale from 1 to 10?

[patient] I’d say it’s about a 6 or 7. It’s not unbearable, but it’s definitely affecting my daily life.

[doctor] Have you experienced any chest pain or palpitations?

[patient] No, none of that.

[doctor] Any shortness of breath?

[patient] No.

[doctor] How about any abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting?

[patient] No, I haven’t had any of those either.

[doctor] Are you having any pain or burning when you urinate?

[patient] No, just going a lot more than usual.

[doctor] And how about headaches or dizziness?

[patient] No headaches or dizziness. Just trouble concentrating.

[doctor] Hmm, okay. Let’s talk a little bit about your medical history. I see that you have prediabetes and hypertension. How have you been managing those conditions?

[patient] I take Lisinopril for my blood pressure, and I’ve been trying to watch my diet because of the prediabetes.

[doctor] Alright, and are you currently taking any other medications besides Lisinopril?

[patient] No, just the Lisinopril.

[doctor] Okay, thank you for that information. Let’s move on to a quick physical exam. I’m going to check your vital signs and do a general examination. 

[doctor] Your blood pressure is 140/85 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 16, and your temperature is 98.6°F. You appear a bit fatigued. 

[patient] Yeah, that sounds about right.

[doctor] Let me check your head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat. Everything looks normal, no lesions or abnormalities. Your heart sounds regular, no murmurs. Your lungs are clear to auscultation. Your abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there are no signs of organ enlargement.

[patient] Okay.

[doctor] Your extremities show no edema, and your peripheral pulses are intact. Neurologically, you are alert and oriented with no focal deficits. 

[patient] That’s good to know.

[doctor] Based on your symptoms and your history of prediabetes, it’s likely that you might be experiencing hyperglycemia, which can be a sign of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. 

[patient] Oh no, that doesn’t sound good.

[doctor] It’s okay, we can manage this. I’d like to start you on Metformin 500 mg, twice daily with meals. It’s important to take this medication regularly, and you might experience some gastrointestinal side effects initially.

[patient] What kind of side effects?

[doctor] You might have some stomach upset or diarrhea, but these usually improve over time. If it becomes too bothersome, let me know. We can adjust the dose if needed.

[patient] Okay, I’ll try it.

[doctor] I also recommend some lifestyle modifications. We’ll work together with a registered dietitian to help you reduce your carbohydrate intake and increase fiber in your diet. 

[patient] That sounds like a big change.

[doctor] I understand it can be daunting, but it’s crucial for managing your condition. We’ll also encourage you to increase your physical activity. Even a 30-minute walk five days a week can make a big difference.

[patient] I’ll try my best.

[doctor] Great, and if you smoke, I highly recommend quitting. We can provide resources to help with that.

[patient] I don’t smoke, so that’s one less thing to worry about.

[doctor] That’s good to hear. I’d also like you to start monitoring your blood glucose levels at home. This will help us track your progress and make any necessary adjustments.

[patient] How often should I check my blood sugar?

[doctor] We’ll start with checking it once in the morning before breakfast and once two hours after a meal. We can adjust the frequency based on your readings.

[patient] Alright, I can do that.

[doctor] I’d like to see you again in three months for a follow-up appointment to evaluate how you’re doing and to possibly adjust your medication. 

[patient] Okay, I’ll set up the appointment.

[doctor] I’ll also refer you to a registered dietitian for more comprehensive dietary management. We’ll schedule some lab tests today, including a comprehensive metabolic panel, Hemoglobin A1c, and a lipid profile. We’ll review the results at your next appointment.

[patient] Alright, I’ll get those done.

[doctor] Lastly, let’s talk about diabetes and its management. It’s important to understand that lifestyle changes and adherence to treatment are key. 

[patient] I know, it’s just a lot to take in.

[doctor] I understand. We’ll provide you with educational materials on diabetes and nutrition that are easy to understand. You’re not alone in this, and we’re here to support you.

[patient] Thank you. That helps a lot.

[doctor] Do you have any questions or concerns about the treatment plan?

[patient] Not right now. I just hope I can manage to make these changes.

[doctor] You can do it, and we’re here to help you every step of the way. Remember, if you have any questions or concerns, please don’t hesitate to reach out.

[patient] Thank you, doctor.

[doctor] You’re welcome, Ms. Gomez. Take care, and I’ll see you in three months.

[patient] See you then, doctor.
```
